title: Deep-Vein Thrombosis and Pulmonary Embolism
specialty: Emergency Medicine, Internal Medicine and Haematology

evidenceAudit.scope: Non-pregnant adults with suspected or confirmed lower-limb DVT or acute PE (pregnancy notes included). Verified against the Saudi MOH PE (2022) and DVT (2024) protocols and the ESC/ERS 2019 PE guideline as summarised by its chairs.
findings: Thrombolysis dose taken from the alteplase product information because neither MOH protocol nor the ESC summary states it.
Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 12 Oct 2026.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: Local formulary availability and hospital protocol adoption

pathophysiology.summary: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) is clot formation in the deep veins, usually of the leg, which can break off and obstruct the pulmonary arteries. A large obstruction raises right ventricular afterload; the right ventricle dilates and fails, causing obstructive shock.
keyMechanisms: Virchow's triad of stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability drives clot formation; provoking factors include surgery, immobilisation, cancer, pregnancy and hormones.
Proximal (popliteal and above) DVT carries the main embolic risk; distal DVT can extend proximally.
PE obstructs pulmonary flow, causing V/Q mismatch and hypoxaemia, raised pulmonary pressure and right ventricular strain (raised troponin and natriuretic peptides, RV dilatation on echo or CT).
Haemodynamic collapse (high-risk PE) comes from right ventricular failure and falling left ventricular filling.
Recurrence risk depends on whether the event was provoked by a major transient factor, unprovoked, or due to persistent factors (cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome).

symptoms: DVT: unilateral leg pain, swelling, warmth.
PE: breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, syncope or pre-syncope (all non-specific).
physicalSigns: DVT: calf or thigh swelling and tenderness, distended superficial veins.
PE: tachycardia, tachypnoea, hypoxia; signs of DVT; hypotension or shock in high-risk PE.
Signs of right heart strain: raised JVP.
redFlags: Haemodynamic instability = high-risk PE: cardiac arrest; obstructive shock (SBP below 90 or vasopressors needed despite filling, with end-organ hypoperfusion); or persistent hypotension (SBP below 90 or a drop of 40 mmHg or more for more than 15 min)
Bedside echo showing RV dysfunction in a highly unstable patient is enough to give immediate reperfusion
Active bleeding or absolute contraindication to anticoagulation: consider an IVC filter
precipitants: Major surgery (general anaesthesia over 30 min), immobilisation 3 days or more, trauma or leg plaster.
Pregnancy and postpartum; hormonal contraception or HRT.
Active cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome, thrombophilia, myeloproliferative disease.
Prolonged travel over 12 h; acute infection.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Ischaemic ECG changes and troponin pattern; regional wall-motion abnormality.
Tearing pain, pulse or BP differential, widened mediastinum; CT aortogram.
Consolidation or pneumothorax on imaging; fever.

differentials.condition: Cellulitis, ruptured Baker's cyst, muscle injury (for DVT)

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Only in non-high clinical probability, after a validated pre-test probability score
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Normal D-dimer with non-high probability excludes PE without CT. ESC: consider age-adjusted cut-off (age × 10 µg/L above 50 years) or the YEARS rule (no YEARS items and D-dimer below 1000 ng/mL, or 1 or more items and below 500 ng/mL).

clinicalManagement.title: Assess probability and start anticoagulation early
actions: Stabilise first. Use a validated pre-test probability score with D-dimer in stable patients.

Start anticoagulation before confirmation if suspicion is high, or intermediate with results delayed over 4 h, or low with results delayed over 24 h (MOH), unless bleeding or an absolute contraindication.
Bedside echo now; if RV dysfunction and no alternative cause, treat as high-risk PE.

clinicalManagement.title: Respiratory and haemodynamic support
actions: Oxygen to SpO2 at least 90% (MOH); intubate for severe hypoxaemia, collapse or respiratory failure.
Hypotension: small fluid volumes (500–1000 mL 0.9% saline), then noradrenaline if perfusion does not improve; dobutamine sometimes for low output.

clinicalManagement.title: High-risk (massive) PE: reperfusion
actions: Systemic thrombolysis is first-line: alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 h (product information). Use UFH infusion with thrombolysis.
Contraindication to thrombolysis: surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed treatment where available; ECMO only as a bridge.
Intermediate-risk PE: no routine thrombolysis; monitor and give rescue thrombolysis if decompensating.

clinicalManagement.title: Stratify stable PE
actions: Intermediate risk: RV strain on imaging and/or raised troponin or BNP → admit, monitor, anticoagulate.
Low risk: sPESI 0 or no Hestia criteria, and no RV dysfunction or right heart thrombus → consider early discharge on a DOAC.
sPESI items (1 point each): age above 80, cancer, chronic cardiopulmonary disease, HR 110 or more, SBP below 100, SpO2 below 90%.

clinicalManagement.title: Choose the anticoagulant
actions: Stable patients: a DOAC is preferred over warfarin (ESC). Apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily.

Parenteral options: enoxaparin 1 mg/kg every 12 h (or 1.5 mg/kg every 24 h); IV UFH 80 units/kg bolus then 18 units/kg/h to target aPTT (preferred if unstable, severe renal failure or thrombolysis planned); fondaparinux by weight (5, 7.5 or 10 mg daily).
Warfarin: overlap with a parenteral agent for at least 5 days and until INR is 2 or more for 2 days; target INR 2–3.
Dabigatran: only after at least 5 days of a parenteral agent.
LMWH, or edoxaban or rivaroxaban (caution in GI cancer).
Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg every 24 h; fondaparinux contraindicated; avoid DOACs in severe renal impairment; UFH or warfarin.
LMWH (single-dose prefilled syringes); no DOACs or warfarin.
Warfarin (VKA) rather than DOAC.

branches.condition: Isolated distal DVT, no severe symptoms or extension risk
actions: Serial ultrasound for 2 weeks without anticoagulation; anticoagulate if it extends (MOH).

clinicalManagement.title: Duration
actions: All patients at least 3 months.
Provoked by a major transient factor: stop at 3 months.
Unprovoked or persistent risk: consider extended treatment, reassessed at least yearly; after 6 months apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily (or rivaroxaban 10 mg daily) may be used.
Second VTE, cancer or antiphospholipid syndrome: indefinite (while bleeding risk allows).

learningObjectives: Recognise, investigate and manage deep-vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism in the emergency department.

keyPoints: Unstable = high-risk PE: bedside echo, then thrombolysis (alteplase 100 mg over 2 h).
Start anticoagulation on suspicion when probability is intermediate or high.
DOAC preferred for most stable patients; LMWH in pregnancy; VKA in antiphospholipid syndrome.
Assess the RV before early discharge.
At least 3 months of anticoagulation; decide on extension at review.
pitfalls: Using DOACs in pregnancy, severe renal impairment or antiphospholipid syndrome.
Stopping warfarin bridging before INR is 2 or more for 2 days.
Discharging without checking the right ventricle.

patientEducation: How to take the anticoagulant and why adherence matters; bleeding warning signs.
Return immediately with worsening breathlessness, chest pain or bleeding.
Stop oestrogen-containing contraception after PE on it; discuss alternatives.
lifestyleAndDiet: Not applicable in the acute phase.
mdtReferrals: PE response or multidisciplinary team for high-risk and selected intermediate-risk PE.
Haematology for thrombophilia, recurrent VTE or anticoagulation problems.
Pulmonary hypertension centre if CTEPH suspected at follow-up.
dischargeCriteria: Haemodynamically stable, no oxygen or IV analgesia needed.
sPESI 0 or no Hestia criteria and no RV dysfunction (for early discharge).
Anticoagulant supplied and taught; adequate support at home.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review at 3 months to decide on extended anticoagulation; check for recurrence, bleeding and cancer; if breathlessness persists, echo and BNP to look for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension.

adjustments: Contraindicated: active internal bleeding, recent stroke, intracranial or intraspinal surgery or serious head trauma within 3 months, intracranial lesions, bleeding diathesis, severe uncontrolled hypertension
